html:
It’s often claimed that strict exercise technique is essential for maximizing hypertrophy. But what does the research actually show?

Our review of literature on the topic, led by @pakpatroklos, provides evidence-based insights into how different aspects of resistance training technique influence muscle growth (PMID: 38249086).

Here are some key takeaways:

--Training through a full ROM generally appears beneficial for hypertrophy, although partial repetitions performed at longer muscle lengths may produce comparable or potentially superior results in some circumstances.

--A relatively wide range of repetition durations can effectively promote hypertrophy. Deliberately slowing repetitions does not appear to provide additional benefits, and excessively slow repetitions may be counterproductive.

-- Regarding body positioning and movement patterns, fundamental biomechanical principles should guide exercise technique to ensure proper loading of the target muscles. However, individual differences in anatomy, limb proportions, flexibility, and other factors should be considered when determining optimal technique.

--Standardizing technique can help ensure that changes in training performance reflect actual progress rather than alterations in how an exercise is performed.

Bottom line: Exercise technique matters, but there is no single universally optimal way to perform every exercise for muscle growth. Current evidence supports using a relatively large ROM, controlling the load, and maintaining a consistent movement pattern. Many finer aspects of exercise technique remain understudied and should be individualized based on personal abilities, comfort, and biomechanics.

title: [X @BradSchoenfeld] 2026-10-31 21:37 KST Many lifters rely on the sensation of muscl
html:
Many lifters rely on the sensation of muscle contraction to determine whether an exercise is effectively targeting that muscle. But how accurately does this subjective sensation reflect actual muscle activation?

A new study provides interesting insights on the topic (PMID: 42958421) The researchers recruited 9 trained men who performed leg curls at three different hip flexion angles (0, 40, and 80 degrees). Each condition involved 5 sets of 10 repetitions at 70% of 1RM.
